problem: Zero-shot MLLM-based VLN methods invoke large multimodal models with autoregressive generation at every step, giving high latency and API cost, even though the final decision is just a choice among a few waypoints or Stop.
motivation: Each VLN step is inherently a structured selection over a small finite action set, so repeated multimodal text generation is a mismatch and limits real-time responsiveness. Jev offers typed probabilistic choice over textual states without token generation, but needs compact text states, which requires compressing visual observations while preserving discriminative cues.
key_idea: Compress each candidate waypoint's view into a compact text action description (geometry + BLIP caption + RAM tags), filter shared semantics and keep action-specific memory, then let Jev make a typed Choice decision instead of generating text with an MLLM.
insight: Most of the gain comes from making the text state discriminative: adding DASM (common-tag filtering plus semantic history) raises SR from 21.0 to 27.0 and SPL from 16.1 to 22.4, more than adding RAM tags (19.0 to 21.0 SR). Under the same ACVC-DASM state, Jev beats GPT-4o (14.0 SR) and Qwen3.8-Max (25.0 SR) with reasoning disabled, at lower latency and cost. Failure analysis shows 60 of 73 failures are wrong waypoint selection, i.e. fine-grained spatial relations remain the bottleneck.
method: Waypoint candidates: pretrained SmartWay waypoint predictor (DINOv2 RGB + depth, cross-attention, Transformer) gives a heatmap of 120 heading bins and 12 distance bins; NMS keeps up to 5 waypoints, each with the nearest RGB sub-view.

ACVC: for each candidate, BLIP produces a caption and RAM produces semantic tags, bound to the motion description (e.g. turn slight left), heading and distance as Z=(m,θ,d,C,R); duplicate views are processed once, and BLIP and RAM run in parallel in batch.
DASM Common-Tag Filtering: the intersection G of RAM tags across all candidates is kept once as shared scene context and removed from each action's tag set, giving discriminative D=(m,θ,d,C,R~).
DASM history: after each executed action, its motion, heading, distance, caption and filtered tags are appended to the history H, giving state S=(H,G,{D}).

Typed decision (Jev): the instruction, S and option-labelled actions (waypoints + Stop) are passed to Jev via its official API; it outputs a probabilistic Choice with no autoregressive generation, and the chosen waypoint (θ,d) goes to the continuous controller.
Real-world deployment: wheeled robot with Insta360 X4 panoramic camera, CLASH-style clustering waypoint extraction, same ACVC-DASM-Jev pipeline.

setting.backbone: Jev (typed decision model, API) + BLIP + RAM + pretrained SmartWay waypoint predictor (all used as is)
setting.observation: panoramic RGB-D (12 views at 30°), converted into text
setting.action_space: predicted waypoints (up to 5 candidates, heading + distance) plus Stop, executed by a continuous controller

results: NavJev reaches 27.0 SR / 22.4 SPL at 0.65 s/step, beating Open-Nav (GPT-4o) at 19.0/16.1 and roughly matching SmartWay's SPL (22.5), though SmartWay has higher SR (29.0) and OSR (51.0). P2DNav (50.0 SR, 30.6 SPL) and supervised methods are much stronger. It is 41.5× faster than Open-Nav, 8.2× than SmartWay and 7.6× than P2DNav, with API cost of $0.06 per 100 episodes versus $2.19 for Qwen3.8-Max and $3.67 for GPT-4o.
limitations: Absolute accuracy is low: OSR 35.0 and NE 7.48 are worse than SmartWay and P2DNav, and it is far below supervised methods; evaluated on only 100 episodes.
82.2% of failures are wrong waypoint selection, since fine-grained spatial relations in instructions are lost in caption/tag text compression.
Depends on the external Jev API (82.5% of latency) and on a pretrained waypoint predictor; the real-world test is small (20 tasks) and compared only to one baseline.
